summary:
Celestial Baymax is a working, local astronaut-health monitoring prototype that connects medical history, health observations, explainable screening, guided follow-up and mission review. It helps a crew member answer four practical questions: What has changed? Why does it matter? What information is missing? What should happen next?

Using fictional astronaut profiles and clearly labelled simulated or manually entered observations, the application presents health trends, identifies demonstration screening flags, explains the supporting evidence and preserves a continuing case timeline. Its Deep Space Link simulator explores how a structured health handover can remain useful when communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable.

NASA Human Research Program and Canadian Space Agency resources inform the spaceflight context and reference explanations. The prototype runs locally without physical sensors or paid AI APIs. Its conversational assistant uses predefined explanation logic. Screening rules are transparent demonstration assumptions, not clinically validated predictions; diagnosis, treatment decisions and medical clearance remain with authorized personnel.
details:
Predict. Prevent. Protect. Recover.

The problem

During an extended mission, noticing a changed health indicator is only the beginning. A crew member also needs to understand its context, repeat or complete missing measurements, document what was done, identify concerns requiring review and communicate a coherent case to medical personnel.

Celestial Baymax explores how software can connect these tasks when immediate ground support is unavailable.

Our solution

Celestial Baymax is a functioning software prototype organized around one continuing workflow:

Medical history → Health monitoring → Explainable screening → Guided checks → Prevention and care-support information → Mission review → Handover and recovery monitoring.

Crew history and monitoring

The demonstration includes six fictional astronauts with different medical histories. Users can create, edit, search, archive and restore profiles.

The dashboard brings together observations such as heart rate, oxygen saturation, sleep, stress, fatigue and exercise. It displays trends, units, timestamps, sources and data freshness. Missing or older records are visible rather than silently interpreted as normal results.

Explainable screening and guided follow-up

A shared rule engine screens eight domains: cardiovascular health, bone health, muscle health, sleep, fatigue, vision, stress and respiratory health.

Results identify supporting observations, relevant history, uncertainty, rule identifiers and suggested follow-up. Guided checks turn an information gap into an actionable measurement or question. Continuing case timelines preserve observations, notes and subsequent changes.

Prevention, support and understandable explanations

The application connects screening concerns to educational prevention and follow-up information.

Its conversational assistant answers questions about the selected astronaut and explains why a category was assigned or what information is needed next. Responses are generated locally through predefined logic, without a paid API or runtime generative language model.

Care-support information is educational and does not constitute approved mission treatment protocols.

Mission review

Users configure mission destination, duration, activities, workload and EVA requirements. A prioritized crew table uses four categories:

- Priority Review.

- Review Before Assignment.

- More Data Needed.

- No Demo Flags.

The interface identifies the inputs and assumptions influencing the review. “No Demo Flags” does not mean medical clearance. The application never independently declares a crew member medically fit or permanently unfit for flight.

Deep Space Link and continuing cases

A local communication simulator models queued and delayed handovers, link outages and fictional ground replies.

A frozen evidence snapshot records what was known when a handover was created, while the continuing case timeline preserves later developments. This demonstrates how a health concern progresses through follow-up and simulated ground review instead of ending at an alert.

Deep Space Link is a software simulation, not an operational communications service.

Mission evidence, radiation and cabin context

Additional records capture mission context, radiation observations and cabin conditions with source labels and observation times.

Radiation records preserve their quantity and original units. Absorbed dose and dose equivalent remain distinct. The application does not estimate an individual’s cancer probability, calculate medical safe limits or connect to radiation-monitoring hardware.

Demonstration scenarios and data integration

Six scenarios demonstrate normal observations, sleep deprivation, cardiovascular strain, vision changes, reduced exercise and recovery.

Generated observations are labelled simulated and stored separately from baseline records, with replay and comparisons.

CSV/JSON importing supports preview, suggested and manual column mapping, validation, duplicate handling and error reporting. The importer is adaptable; dataset-specific adapters may still be required for future external datasets.

What makes the approach distinctive

The main contribution is continuity between evidence and action.

One screening engine supplies the dashboard, assistant, mission review and case workflow. A concern remains connected to the measurement that triggered it, the uncertainty around it, the next check and the subsequent handover.

Data freshness and unknown information receive explicit attention. Deep Space Link adds a mission-specific demonstration of maintaining a coherent health record while ground support is delayed.

Technical implementation

The submitted Windows/SQLite edition uses TypeScript, React, Expo/React Native Web, NativeWind, Node.js, Express, tRPC and Drizzle ORM with local SQLite storage.

It includes complete source code, a packaged browser/API build, Windows setup/start launchers, fictional demonstration records, automated tests and CSV/JSON/SQLite exports.

Local owner access uses a passphrase and expiring sessions. The prototype database is not encrypted at rest, so the demonstration uses fictional records.

Testing and current status

The packaged edition passed TypeScript checks, 46 automated tests and 25 portable release checks in a Linux environment.

Checks included persistence after restart, owner sessions, imports, simulation separation, concurrent evidence handling, backup validity and database integrity. One original starter authentication placeholder test remains skipped.

Native Windows launcher execution was not verified in that environment. These checks verify software behavior, not clinical accuracy, astronaut usability or operational mission readiness.

Intended impact and next steps

The intended benefit is clearer, more traceable crew health review and more complete communication with medical teams.

Future work would require evaluation with space-medicine and human-factors specialists, validated screening thresholds, appropriate dataset adapters, privacy and security improvements, and representative user testing.

Any future machine-learning model would require suitable training data and independent validation before clinical claims could be made.

Limitations

All astronaut profiles and health observations in the demonstration are fictional or simulated. NASA/CSA publications provide scientific background, not patient records or validation of the application’s numeric cutoffs.

Exercise logs do not measure bone density or muscle mass; reported vision changes do not diagnose SANS.

Celestial Baymax does not diagnose illness, prescribe medication, provide medical clearance, replace a flight surgeon or claim NASA/CSA endorsement.
